Over the past four weeks, global equity markets have succumbed to a recurring bout of cognitive dissonance. Macro cyclical allocators, traditional tech sell-side analysts, and cyclical hedge fund desks have driven the forward price-to-earnings multiples of leading memory producers—Micron Technology ($MU) and SK Hynix (000660.KS)—down into the 3.0x to 4.5x range
The intellectual justification for this valuation collapse is built entirely on historical trauma. Market participants look back at the brutal downcycles of 2018 and 2022, asserting with cynical certainty that "memory has been boom and bust since the 1970s, long-term agreements (LTAs) are meaningless paper, and customers will walk away the moment spot prices weaken.
This monograph demonstrates that this short thesis is built on an elementary category error: it applies legacy commodity DRAM economic models to an industry that has physically mutated into custom advanced logic foundry manufacturing
In Monograph #03: The 3:1 Wafer Squeeze, we established the solid-state manufacturing laws that govern HBM4: the irreversible cleanroom footprint of Through-Silicon Vias (TSV), the exponential yield degradation across 16-high stacks, and the thermo-mechanical warpage limits of Navier-Cauchy elasticity that forced the entire industry into TSMC's packaging ecosystem
This monograph serves as the direct sequel and ultimate commercial verdict. We prove that the structural break in memory is not merely a supply-side physical bottleneck, but a total destruction of spot market fungibility:
1. The Extinction of Spot Market Arbitrage: Unlike DDR3 or DDR4, which adhered to standardized JEDEC pinouts and could be sourced generically off spot exchanges in Shenzhen or Taipei, HBM4 features a 2,048-bit wide physical bus fabricated on TSMC's 3nm/4nm advanced logic nodes. Its microbump pinout, PHY routing, and Built-In Self-Test (BIST) circuitry are co-designed and taped out exclusively for specific accelerator architectures (such as Nvidia Vera Rubin or Google TPU). There is no spot market for custom logic dies.
2. The "Hostage Silicon" Contractual Lock: A hyperscaler attempting to breach an HBM4 take-or-pay agreement cannot simply substitute generic components. Walking away forfeits the entire custom logic tape-out, stranding tens of thousands of host GPUs and writing off billions in advanced packaging commitments. The default penalty is not a price adjustment; it is the death of the compute cluster itself.
3. The 816B Agentic Workload Mandate: Empirical telemetry from next-generation inference benchmarks (such as SemiAnalysis's preview of Vera Rubin running Muse Spark Open 816B) reveals that agentic reasoning loops and multi-turn context windows shift compute entirely into the memory-bandwidth-bound decode phase. Delivering 1,000 tokens/sec/user at P90 interactivity requires sustained bandwidth exceeding 20 TB/s per socket—a physical regime that only 2,048-bit custom HBM4 can service.
4. The Refutation of the 10% Revenue Myth: Bearish arguments claiming that HBM accounts for only 10% of memory revenue suffer from basic arithmetic errors that conflate total addressable market (TAM) with company-specific revenue. In a $100B 2027 HBM market, a 20% share generates $20B for Micron, representing ~40% of its consensus $50B top line and over 60% of total gross profit. Compounded by the 3.5:1 wafer crowd-out ratio, allocating 15% of bit production to HBM consumes over 40% of leading-edge wafer starts, locking commodity server DDR5 into an irreversible 20% to 22% structural supply deficit.
5. The Multiple Rerating: When non-cancellable custom silicon agreements eliminate downside cash flow volatility, treating memory producers as 3x P/E cyclicals represents the single largest valuation dislocation in modern semiconductor history. Applying an infrastructure cash flow discount rate (WACC compression from 11.5% to 7.5%) dictates a fundamental rerating toward 15x to 20x P/E, triggering a generational Davis Double Play.
Chapter I. The 3x P/E Fallacy: Commodity PTSD vs. Custom Foundry Reality
1.1 The Anatomy of the 2018 Trauma
To understand why Wall Street is currently mispricing memory stocks, one must examine the psychological scar tissue of the 2018–2019 collapse.
In late 2017, memory producers enjoyed peak operating margins exceeding 60%. Hyperscalers had engaged in panic buying of standard server DDR4 DIMMs. However, by mid-2018, as enterprise server demand cooled, cloud procurement desks abruptly halted purchasing.
Because DDR4 was a standardized commodity governed by JEDEC specifications, memory modules were 100% fungible:
• A 64GB DDR4-2666 ECC Registered DIMM produced by Samsung was electrically and physically interchangeable with an equivalent module produced by Micron or SK Hynix.
• When spot market prices dropped below contract prices, cloud buyers immediately breached verbal commitments, allowed existing inventories to burn down, and sourced distressed lots from the spot market at cash cost.
• Within four quarters, operating margins collapsed from +60% to single digits, and memory equities experienced peak-to-trough drawdowns of 40% to 55%.
Today's macro bears assume this exact sequence will replay in 2027. They point to forward multiples of 3.5x for Micron and 4.0x for SK Hynix as evidence that "smart money" is already pricing in the inevitable margin liquidation.
🔄 Commodity Memory vs. Bespoke AI Silicon Regime Comparison:
* Traditional Commodity DRAM Regime (DDR3 / DDR4 / Standard DDR5):
* Standard JEDEC Sockets → 100% Interchangeable Fungibility → High Spot Liquidity
* Downcycle Reality: Spot price crumbles → LTAs breached → Severe margin bust (2018)
* Modern AI Memory Regime (HBM3e / HBM4 / Custom Base Dies):
* Custom Silicon Tape-Out → Zero Spot Fungibility → Bilateral Monopoly Lock-in
* Downcycle Reality: Bespoke pinouts → Default scraps $50k+ GPU SiP → Cash flows intact (2027+)
1.2 The Fallacy of Applying Commodity Elasticity to Heterogeneous SiP
The flaw in this thesis lies in the assumption of product interchangeability.
A commodity market requires two prerequisites:
1. Standardized form factors allowing multiple suppliers to compete for an identical socket.
2. Low switching costs enabling buyers to arbitrage price differentials across vendors.
In HBM4, both prerequisites are physically non-existent. HBM4 is not an independent component sold on a circuit board; it is an integrated sub-element of a System-in-Package (SiP).
When an accelerator manufacturer like Nvidia or Google designs an ultra-high-performance package, the physical placement of the HBM cubes, the interposer routing lines, the microbump metallurgy, and the custom PHY layer inside the base die are finalized 24 months prior to mass production.
There is no secondary spot market for HBM4. You cannot buy an HBM4 stack from an open distributor, nor can an unallocated stack produced for an Nvidia Vera Rubin module be redirected to an AMD Helios chassis or a custom hyperscaler ASIC.
Pricing an asset class with zero secondary market liquidity and 100% bilateral co-design at a commodity cyclical multiple is an analytical failure.
Chapter II. The "Hostage Silicon" Mechanism: Co-Design, TSMC Base Dies & Contractual Lock-in
2.1 The Metamorphosis of the Logic Base Die
In earlier generations (HBM2e and HBM3), the base die at the bottom of the memory stack was manufactured by the memory vendors themselves using mature DRAM-adjacent processes (1y/1z nm). Its function was largely passive: simple test logic, power routing, and basic signal buffering.
With HBM4, the physical bus width doubles from 1,024 bits to 2,048 bits. This dramatic expansion in interconnect density requires over 40,000 microbumps per cube at an ultra-fine pitch of 25 µm to 30 µm. A standard DRAM process cannot achieve the routing density or the switching speeds required to drive 2,048 differential lines at multi-gigabit rates while maintaining low bit-error rates (BER).
Consequently, the industry has executed an irreversible structural shift: the HBM4 base die has migrated entirely to leading-edge foundry logic nodes—predominantly TSMC N3E and N4P.

2.2 The Hostage Calculus: Default Economics
This transition changes the contract law of memory procurement.
Consider the economic reality of a hyperscaler that has entered into a multi-billion-dollar long-term agreement (LTA) with SK Hynix or Micron for HBM4:
1. Foundry Commitment: The memory maker does not order base die wafers from TSMC on speculation. Base die wafer starts at TSMC's N3 fabs require non-refundable engineering deposits, dedicated photomask sets, and binding advanced packaging slots (CoWoS-L) booked 12 to 18 months in advance.
2. Proprietary Pinout Alignment: The physical pad array of the TSMC N3 base die is matched to the sub-micron design rules of the host accelerator's silicon interposer.
3. The Penalty of Default: If a cloud customer experiences softening demand and attempts to breach the HBM4 agreement:
• The customer cannot source alternative memory because no competitor manufactures an HBM4 stack with an identical custom logic base die layout.
• Cancelling the memory allocation halts the advanced packaging line at TSMC or ASE, idling the compute dies (GPUs/XPUs) already fabricated.
• A single compute tray in a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack carries a bill-of-materials exceeding $250,000. Idling an entire rack deployment over an HBM dispute results in an immediate capital loss orders of magnitude larger than any conceivable savings from memory renegotiation.

Chapter III. The Agentic Decode Limit: 816B Parameters, 1,000 tok/s Interactivity & The 20 TB/s Memory Wall
3.1 Workload Transitions: From Training Batch Sizes to Single-User Decode
The second intellectual foundation of the bear thesis is the assertion that "model training is saturating, pre-training clusters are fully built, and inference requires far less memory bandwidth."
This view reflects an outdated understanding of AI workloads, anchored in dense model batch processing. In reality, the migration toward Agentic AI—autonomous systems executing multi-turn tool use, continuous code generation, and iterative reasoning loops—has inverted the compute-to-memory ratio.
In agentic workflows, the user interaction model is governed by interactivity latency (Time-to-First-Token and Time-per-Output-Token):
• A software developer using an agentic coding assistant cannot wait for a batch of 64 requests to assemble. The agent must execute sequential inference at a batch size of N = 1 or N = 2.
• The inference cycle splits into two fundamentally distinct phases: Prefill (compute-bound) and Decode (memory-bandwidth-bound).
📐 Agentic Decode Arithmetic Intensity Formula:
Arithmetic Intensity (Decode) = FLOPs / Bytes Transferred ≈ (2 × P × B) / [ (2 × P × B) + (2 × L × D_model × B) ] ≪ 1.0 FLOPs/Byte
(where P = Model Parameter Count, B = Batch Size, L = Context Sequence Length, D_model = Hidden State Dimension)
During the generation of each new token in a large model, the entire weight tensor of the model, alongside the accumulated Key-Value (KV) cache of the conversation, must be read out of memory:
⚡ Minimum Sustained Memory Bandwidth Formula:
Required Memory Bandwidth = [ Model Parameters (Bytes) × Tokens per Second ] / Hardware Operational Efficiency
⚙️ Computational Bottleneck Shift in Frontier Agentic Models:
* Prefill Phase (Prompt Processing):
* Governing Bound: Compute-bound (Tensor Core FLOPs)
* Underlying Physics: Massive dense matrix multiplications (GEMM)
* Primary Hardware Target: Raw TFLOPS per Watt
* Decode Phase (Token-by-Token Autoregressive Generation):
* Governing Bound: Memory-bandwidth-bound (HBM bus saturation)
* Underlying Physics: Memory vector-matrix operations (GEMV) + continuous KV cache streaming
* Primary Hardware Target: Terabytes/sec sustained memory bandwidth (HBM4 mandate)
3.2 The SemiAnalysis Vera Rubin InferenceX Telemetry
Empirical data released by SemiAnalysis on November 5, 2026, benchmarked the upcoming Vera Rubin NVL72 platform running the Muse Spark Open 816B Agentic model under its InferenceX evaluation suite.
The results settle the debate regarding memory bandwidth saturation:
Hopper (H100 / H200)• Memory Subsystem Architecture: 80GB–141GB HBM3 / HBM3e• Sustained Memory Bandwidth: 3.35 – 4.8 TB/s• P90 Interactivity Latency Frontier: Collapses sharply at ~90 tokens/sec
Blackwell Ultra (GB300)• Memory Subsystem Architecture: 288GB HBM3e (1,024-bit Bus)• Sustained Memory Bandwidth: ~8.0 TB/s• P90 Interactivity Latency Frontier: Collapses sharply at ~320 tokens/sec
Vera Rubin (NVL72)• Memory Subsystem Architecture: HBM4 (2,048-bit TSMC N3 Base Die)• Sustained Memory Bandwidth: >20.0 TB/s• P90 Interactivity Latency Frontier: Sustains >1,000 tokens/sec/user
Under Hopper and Blackwell Ultra (GB300), the P90 interactivity curve plummets once user latency requirements exceed 250 tokens/sec. The compute cores sit completely idle, waiting for the weights of the 816-billion-parameter network and the KV cache to transfer across the 1,024-bit bus.
Only the Vera Rubin architecture—by transitioning to 2,048-bit HBM4 with active TSMC N3 base dies delivering >20 TB/s per GPU—sustains an interactivity frontier exceeding 1,000 tokens/sec/user, while pushing the overall economic efficiency to 140 million tokens per dollar of Total Cost of Ownership (TCO).
The investment takeaway is stark: In an agentic deployment environment, memory bandwidth is not a secondary specification; it is the sole physical determinant of inference economics.
Hyperscalers cannot reduce HBM procurement without directly collapsing the user-facing throughput of their generative AI platforms.

Chapter IV. The 3.5:1 Cleanroom Crowd-Out: Refuting the "10% Revenue Myth" & The 22% Server Deficit
4.1 Dismantling the Sell-Side Math Error
A persistent critique circulated by macro bears (and echoed across financial social media) argues that HBM cannot protect memory makers from a broader downturn because "HBM accounts for only ~10% of total revenue."
This argument relies on an elementary confusion between the Total Addressable Market (TAM) of the global semiconductor industry and the specific revenue profile of memory producers.
Consider the actual consensus projections for the calendar year 2027:
• Global HBM Industry TAM: $95B – $105B (consensus midpoint: $100B).
• Micron Technology ($MU) Revenue Consensus: $48B – $52B (midpoint: $50B).
• Micron Expected HBM Market Share: ~20% (conservative floor based on 1b/1c nm qualification).
Performing the actual arithmetic:
📊 Micron 2027 HBM Top-Line Mathematical Audit:
Micron 2027 HBM Revenue = $100B (Industry TAM) × 20% (Conservative Share) = $20B
HBM Revenue Contribution = $20B (HBM) / $50B (Consensus Top Line) = 40.0%
HBM does not represent 10% of Micron's business; it represents 40% of gross revenue.
Furthermore, because HBM commands gross margins between 60% and 68%, compared to 35% to 40% for blended commodity DRAM, its earnings contribution is vastly higher:
💰 Micron 2027 Gross Profit Contribution Audit:
Total Corporate Gross Profit (Consensus 50% Blended Margin) ≈ $25B
HBM Gross Profit Contribution = $20B × 65% (HBM Gross Margin) = $13B
HBM Share of Corporate Gross Profit = $13B / $25B = 52.0%
HBM will generate more than half of Micron's entire corporate gross profit by 2027.

4.2 The 3.5:1 Cleanroom Physics: The Transmission Mechanism
Even if one sets aside the direct financial contribution, the bear thesis ignores the physical transmission mechanism through which HBM stabilizes the commodity DRAM market.
In Monograph #03, we established the baseline 3:1 wafer squeeze ratio. As the industry transitions to 16-high HBM4 stacks utilizing 1c nm DRAM layers, the cleanroom footprint penalty expands to 3.5:1:
🔬 Wafer Area & Lithography Cleanroom Consumption Equation:
* Standard DDR5 Wafer (1b/1c nm):
* Die Area: ~70 mm²
* TSV Lithography Passes: 0
* Thinning / CMP: Standard manufacturing steps
* Net Bit Output Efficiency: 1.0x Base
* 16-Hi HBM4 Silicon Stack:
* Die Area: ~135 mm² (expanded by TSV keep-out zones and custom test PHY)
* TSV Deep Reactive-Ion Etching (DRIE) & Cu Electroplating: Multi-pass high-aspect ratio
* Wafer Backgrinding: Extreme thin-down to 30 µm (critical yield bottleneck)
* Cleanroom Opportunity Cost: 3.5x Standard Wafers Consumed per Bit
Every single wafer allocated to HBM4 permanently removes 3.5 wafer starts from standard server DDR5 and LPDDR5 lines.
Now, consider the macro wafer allocation across the Big-3 memory cleanrooms (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron):
• Total leading-edge DRAM wafer capacity: ~1,550,000 wafer starts per month (WSPM).
• To satisfy the projected 2027 demand of 1.45 billion gigabits of HBM, the industry must allocate approximately 580,000 WSPM of raw wafer starts directly to HBM production lines.
🏭 Global Cleanroom Floor Space Consumption Ratio:
Cleanroom Allocation Ratio = 580,000 WSPM (HBM Starts) / 1,550,000 WSPM (Global Leading-Edge DRAM) = 37.4%
Nearly 40% of all leading-edge cleanroom floor space on planet Earth is physically consumed by HBM manufacturing.
This creates an inescapable physical reality for standard enterprise server memory:
• The remaining cleanroom capacity (~970,000 WSPM) is insufficient to meet baseline cloud server refresh requirements.
• Channel audits across North American and Taiwanese ODMs indicate that enterprise server DDR5 supply is operating with an unbridgeable 20% to 22% structural deficit.
• Even if an enterprise customer refuses to purchase HBM, the prices they pay for standard 64GB and 128GB DDR5 server modules are propelled upward by the shortage induced by HBM manufacturing.
🏭 Global Leading-Edge DRAM Cleanroom Allocation (1,550,000 WSPM Total):
* HBM4 / HBM3e Allocation [580,000 WSPM · 37.4% Floor Space]:
* Yields 15% of global memory bit volume
* Consumes 3.5x wafer area per bit produced
* Commands 62%–68% gross margin
* Standard Enterprise DDR5 Allocation [970,000 WSPM · 62.6% Floor Space]:
* Must supply entire global cloud server refresh
* Structural supply deficit locked at 20%–22%
* Pricing power guaranteed by cleanroom crowd-out

HBM does not need to account for 90% of memory bit volume to govern the market. Through the mathematical reality of cleanroom displacement, HBM acts as a permanent supply drain on the entire semiconductor industry, making a general memory price collapse physically impossible.
Chapter V. The Hierarchical Storage Spillover: CXL 2.0 Pooling, 128TB QLC eSSDs & The Multiple Rerating
5.1 The Emergence of the 3-Tier AI Storage Hierarchy
The extreme cost and physical bandwidth density of HBM4 create a systemic challenge for data center architects: you cannot solve the capacity problem using HBM alone.
A 72-GPU Vera Rubin NVL72 rack contains massive compute density, but the maximum on-package memory capacity is physically capped at roughly 20 TB across the entire rack. However, executing multi-turn agentic workloads with millions of concurrent tokens requires hundreds of terabytes of working memory to store inactive KV cache states.
To prevent high-cost HBM from being consumed by dormant context, hyperscalers are deploying a 3-Tier Solid-State Memory Hierarchy:
Tier 1 (Apex)• Technology Architecture: HBM4 (2,048-bit SiP)• Target Workload Profile: Active attention & layer compute• Sustained Bandwidth Regime: >20,000 GB/s• Dominant Suppliers: SK Hynix, Micron ($MU)
Tier 2 (Near-Line)• Technology Architecture: CXL 2.0 / 3.0 (CMM-D)• Target Workload Profile: Dynamic context & warm KV caching• Sustained Bandwidth Regime: 250 – 500 GB/s• Dominant Suppliers: Samsung Electronics, Micron
Tier 3 (Bulk Cold)• Technology Architecture: PCIe Gen5 QLC eSSD (128TB)• Target Workload Profile: Checkpointing & persistent KV pool• Sustained Bandwidth Regime: 14 – 28 GB/s• Dominant Suppliers: Solidigm (SK Hynix), Samsung
1. Tier 1 (On-Package HBM4): Dedicated purely to active token generation and current layer compute execution (>20 TB/s bandwidth).
2. Tier 2 (CXL 2.0 / 3.0 Memory Pooling): Utilizes Compute Express Link (CXL) memory expansion modules (CMM-D) attached directly to host CPU clusters over PCIe Gen5/Gen6 physical layers. This provides intermediate capacity (256GB to 1TB per socket) at low latencies (<200 nanoseconds), enabling instant paging of warm KV states into HBM.
3. Tier 3 (Ultra-High-Capacity Enterprise QLC eSSDs): Pioneered by SK Hynix's Solidigm subsidiary and Samsung, high-density 61.44TB and 128TB PCIe Gen5 QLC eSSDs are being deployed as near-line cold KV cache storage. Rather than discarding conversation history and re-computing prefill matrices, inference engines serialize dormant KV vectors onto ultra-dense NAND flash.
This 3-tier structure completely invalidates the old sell-side thesis that "AI hardware only benefits HBM while leaving standard flash and DRAM to rot."
The memory supercycle is an integrated solid-state expansion: HBM4 captures the ultra-high-margin silicon apex, while CXL pooling and enterprise QLC eSSDs absorb the high-capacity storage volume at sustained 45% to 50% gross margins.

Chapter VI. The Valuation Arbitrage: The Mathematical Rerating to 15x–20x P/E
6.1 The Cost of Capital Arbitrage
Why does the market assign a 3.5x forward P/E to Micron ($MU) while assigning 30x to Nvidia ($NVDA) and 25x to TSMC ($TSM)?
The discount applied to memory equities is not driven by current earnings; it is driven by the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) and the terminal value fade rate.
Under a standard Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model:
🏛️ Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Valuation Engine:
Enterprise Value = Σ [ FCF_t / (1 + WACC)^t ] + [ Terminal Value / (1 + WACC)^N ]
When an asset is classified as a cyclical commodity:
• Investors assign an elevated equity risk premium to account for the risk that free cash flow drops to zero (or turns negative) in Year 3.
• The applied WACC ranges between 11.5% and 13.0%.
• The terminal growth rate (g) is modeled at 0% or negative, compressing the exit multiple to 5x–6x EV/EBITDA.

Implied Justified Target P/E• Cyclical Commodity Model (Legacy): 4.0x – 6.0x Trough Multiple• Infrastructure Sovereign Model (New Regime): 16.0x – 20.0x Normalised Multiple
When the underlying reality transitions to:
1. Take-or-pay legal contracts extending to 2031–2035;
2. Proprietary custom logic base dies eliminating secondary market supply dumps;
3. Permanent cleanroom crowding guaranteeing structural undersupply in secondary lines;
...the justification for an 12% WACC evaporates. Memory cash flows exhibit the defensive properties of utility infrastructure and proprietary foundry silicon.
Normalizing the WACC to an infrastructure-grade 7.5% to 8.0% mathematically expands the justified target P/E from 4x to between 16x and 20x.
6.2 The Mechanics of the Generational Davis Double Play
A Davis Double Play occurs when a company experiences simultaneous expansion in both underlying earnings per share (EPS revisions) and the valuation multiple assigned to those earnings (P/E expansion):
📈 Davis Double Play Capital Return Equation:
Total Shareholder Return = [ (EPS_Normalized / EPS_Consensus) × (P/E_Target / P/E_Base) ] - 1
Applying conservative, verified parameters for Micron Technology ($MU) through the 2027 cycle:
1. Base Case (Current Market Pricing):
• Consensus FY27 EPS: $12.50 (Assumes cyclical fading).
• Base Multiple: 4.0x Forward P/E.
• Current Stock Price: ~$50 – $55.

Chapter VII. Institutional Conclusion: The Death of the Memory Short
The persistent bearish consensus surrounding leading memory equities is not conservative risk management; it is intellectual obsolescence.
It fails to recognize that:
1. The Spot Market is Dead: HBM4 cannot be arbitrated on an open exchange; its 2,048-bit active logic base die is physically married to specific host accelerators.
2. Breaching Contracts is Suicide: A cloud customer attempting to cancel an HBM allocation scraps their own $50,000+ AI compute trays, creating an unshakeable bilateral hostage lock.
3. Agentic Workloads Guarantee Bandwidth Thirst: Inference models scaling past 800 billion parameters under multi-turn agentic loops are physically gated by memory bandwidth, mandating >20 TB/s per socket.
4. The Cleanroom Math is Inflexible: The 3.5:1 wafer crowd-out permanently drains 40% of global leading-edge wafer starts, starving commodity server DDR5 lines and ensuring multi-year cash flow protection.
Investors pricing Micron ($MU) and SK Hynix at 3x earnings are looking into the rear-view mirror of 2018, mistaking an active computing subsystem for a generic DRAM stick.
When the structural reality of the custom logic transition fully penetrates consensus financial models, the resulting multiple expansion will deliver the most powerful equity rerating across the global semiconductor landscape.

Security Measured In Dollars.

Most chains describe security in bits. QuanChain describes it in dollars.

The cracking-cost model prices an attack on each security level by the cheapest path available to an attacker.

Grover's search looks for an input that hashes to your address. For a 256-bit hash that is about 2^128 quantum operations. The birthday attack, a collision search, is cheaper at about 2^85 operations, though the whitepaper notes it still far exceeds any wallet balance. Shor's attack on the key only applies if a public key is exposed, which child rotation is designed to prevent.

The effective cost is the minimum of the paths that apply, priced at about 5 million dollars per logical qubit-hour.

Bit-strength tells you how hard something is. Dollars tell you whether anyone will do it.
